meta.note: The merged functional inventory. Two corpora existed and barely overlapped: functional-english.json carried DISCURSIVE language (advantages, cause, effect, trends) for essays and reports; functions-corpus.json carried INTERACTIONAL language (thanking, inviting, refusing, advising) for letters and speaking. Seven functions collided and were folded together; the rest are complementary, which is why the merge nearly doubles coverage rather than deduplicating it. FUNCTION is the unit and the browsing axis — a learner looking for a way to disagree politely should not have to know it lives in the essays folder. Categories group the carousel; they do not gate it.
meta.phraseNote: Two phrase shapes, deliberately. Discursive phrases carry a `connector` as well as a stem — 'A major advantage of …' + 'is that it allows people to …, which means …' — because an essay sentence is built in two halves. Interactional phrases are complete as they stand.
meta.registerNote: `register` is set on phrases from functions-corpus and null on those from functional-english, which was never tagged. A card should show the informal-to-formal bar only when its phrases are graded, and a plain list otherwise: showing an axis that is not there would be a lie. Tagging the rest is authoring, and can be done one function at a time.
meta.tasksNote: Questions and cues used to live in two separate files, matched only by their position in an array — so Q2's cue sat at index 4 and the page showed six cards that answered a different question from the one on screen. They are now ONE object per task: topic, question, cue, trigger, models. The pairing is structural and cannot drift again. A task with a question but no cue is a question nobody has written a drill for; a task with a cue but no question is the reverse. Both are visible rather than hidden, because the gaps are the authoring list. The 21 interactional functions — thanking, apologising, refusing, advising — have neither yet.

discursive.label: Weighing it up

reasoning.label: Cause and reason
reasoning.note: Why something happens, and what follows from it.

stance.label: Stance and attitude
stance.note: Positioning yourself towards an idea. Shared with Speaking Part 4.

comparison.label: Comparing
comparison.note: Grammar-bearing — comparative structures are examined in Use of English too.

projecting.label: Likelihood and trends
projecting.note: What might happen, what is broadly true, how things are changing.

social.label: Social moves
social.note: Opening and sustaining a relationship. Heavily conventionalised — where L1 transfer shows first.

interpersonal.label: Asking and responding
interpersonal.note: Adjacency pairs — an invitation expects an acceptance or a refusal.

advisory.label: Advice and suggestion
advisory.note: The advice letter, and Speaking Part 3 collaboration.

planning.label: Plans and arrangements
planning.note: Future forms carry the meaning — present continuous for arrangements.

thanking.label: Thanking

phrases.t: Thank you very much for your help.
I'm most grateful for all you've done.
It was so kind of you to write to me.

thanking.convention: English thanks are short and land early. A Portuguese learner often postpones the thanks to the closing, or expands it; UK convention puts it in the opening line and moves on.

apologising.label: Apologising

phrases.t: I'm very sorry for not writing before.
I apologise for not sending it.
Accept my apologies for being late.

apologising.convention: "I'm afraid" is an apology marker in English, not an expression of fear. It softens bad news and has no direct Portuguese equivalent.

enthusiasm.label: Showing enthusiasm

phrases.t: It was lovely to hear from you.

enthusiasm.convention: Reacting to the reader's news before your own business is close to obligatory in an English informal letter. Omitting it reads as cold, and it is the move Communicative Achievement most often rewards.

phrases.t: What have you got to lose?
You are on the right track.

invitation.label: Inviting

phrases.t: Would you like to stay at my place?
Would you be interested in visiting us?
How about going out on that day?
Do you want to borrow mine?
I wonder if you would like to take ours.

invitation.convention: English invitations are phrased as questions about the reader's wishes, not as statements of the writer's. "I invite you to" is unidiomatic.

offering.label: Offering

phrases.t: If you like, I can give you a lift.
Would you like me to pick you up?
Shall I send it to you again?
How about lunch on that day?

offering.convention: "Shall I…?" is the standard offer form and has no Portuguese parallel; learners reach for "Do you want that I…".

phrases.t: I really look forward to it.

refusing.label: Refusing

phrases.t: I have to turn it down.

refusing.convention: An English refusal opens with the softener and gives the reason after. Leading with the reason sounds like an excuse.

phrases.t: Do you think it would be all right to
What would you say if I
I get mad when she is late.
What annoys me is her hair.

preference.label: Preference

phrases.t: I would rather stay with you.
I wouldn't mind going by bus.
I'd rather you stayed with us.
It doesn't matter if it rains.

preference.convention: "I'd rather you stayed" takes a past form for a present meaning — a structure with no Portuguese equivalent and a recurring Use of English item.

phrases.t: I am not keen on driving.

advice.label: Giving advice

phrases.t: If I were you, I wouldn't buy it.
You ought to take it seriously.
I would advise you to accept it.

advice.convention: Advice to a friend uses second person freely in English. Learners often over-hedge into the impersonal, which weakens the letter.

suggestion.label: Suggesting

phrases.t: It might be a good idea to buy it.
Why don't you contact the manager?
You could always come with us.
You had better let him know.

suggestion.convention: "You had better" carries a warning, not a mild suggestion — stronger than learners usually intend.

requesting_information.label: Requesting information

phrases.t: I would be grateful if you could
I would also like to have
I wonder if you could send me

requesting_information.convention: English politeness sits in the modal — could, would, I wonder if — not in the form of address. A Portuguese learner may open very formally and then make a bare request, which reads as brusque.

ability.label: Ability

phrases.t: I wasn't able to finish it.
He managed to get a new one.

ability.convention: "Managed to" and "succeeded in" both mean achievement against difficulty, and take different structures — to-infinitive against -ing.

phrases.t: I am planning to visit Lisbon.
I'm going to sell my flat.
I would like to visit my family.

making_arrangements.label: Making arrangements

phrases.t: I am arriving in Lisbon at 4.
I am staying at a hotel.
I have arranged to meet my colleagues.
We are flying to Glasgow on the 3rd.

making_arrangements.convention: Fixed arrangements take the present continuous in English, where Portuguese would use a future. "I will arrive at 4" is not wrong but sounds less settled.
